# Every good regulator is a model: what Conant and Ashby mean for AI systems that run themselves

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that an AI agent can manage a system it has no explicit model of, because the model is in its weights. This paper argues otherwise: a regulator is only as good as its model of the thing it regulates. A system that runs itself needs an explicit, current model of its own parts, kept as data it can read and check.

Conant and Ashby argued that the best possible regulator of a system must be, in effect, a model of that system. An AI system that runs a business without an explicit model of its own parts is regulating blind. We check whether this system keeps such a model: a knowledge graph of its own data, declared limits for what it must hold steady, and work items specific enough to be checked.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 3 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

Under broad conditions, the simplest regulator that achieves the best outcome is one whose actions are a mapping of the regulated system's states. In plain terms: good control of a system requires a model of it, and the quality of control is bounded by the quality of the model. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, the model is in the weights, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. A regulator with no model of the regulated system. Each system the platform runs should keep a model of its own data. Here that is the knowledge graph each system builds from its own tables. [1]
2. A model with no stated outcomes to hold. The theorem measures a regulator by the outcomes it keeps. A model is useless for regulation unless the outcomes it serves are declared with limits. [1]
3. Work items too vague to map to a state. If the regulator's actions are a mapping of system states, each action has to name the state it changes and how to check it. A work item without a done check and a live probe is an action mapped to nothing. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [3]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. A regulator with no model of the regulated system: every table becomes graph nodes and edges, kept each pass (DATAGRAPH-1, `seed/worker/src/datagraph.js`); every system has a row, built or pending (DATAGRAPH-1, `doctrine/knowledge-graph.json`)
2. A model with no stated outcomes to hold: essential variables declared with limits (ASHBY-1, `doctrine/ultrastability.json`)
3. Work items too vague to map to a state: fails items with no done check, prediction, out-of-scope line or live probe (SPEC-GATE-1, `seed/scripts/specgate.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. A regulator with no model of the regulated system. Put in place: every table becomes graph nodes and edges, kept each pass. Check it with one number, share of systems in doctrine/knowledge-graph.json whose knowledge graph is built, not pending, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
2. A model with no stated outcomes to hold. Put in place: essential variables declared with limits. Check it with one number, share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json), and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
3. Work items too vague to map to a state. Put in place: fails items with no done check, prediction, out-of-scope line or live probe. Check it with one number, share of open work items with a done check, a prediction, an out-of-scope line and a live proof (foundation/specgate.py), and set a limit for it (>= 0.9 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 2 of 3 of these checks pass today. Share of systems in doctrine/knowledge-graph.json whose knowledge graph is built, not pending reads 1.0 (n = 5; source: doctrine/knowledge-graph.json (declared)). Share of declared essential variables that have limits (doctrine/ultrastability.json) reads 1.0 (n = 19; source: doctrine/ultrastability.json). Share of open work items with a done check, a prediction, an out-of-scope line and a live proof (foundation/specgate.py) reads 0.509 (n = None; source: foundation/specgate.py over docs/issues). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- The theorem is about optimal and simplest regulators. We use it as a design rule, not as proof that this system's model is good enough.
- The graph reading counts systems whose graph is built; it does not measure how faithful each graph is.
- Source. Article, version 1970.
